title: NEOWISE 2014-2024 shows that the 3-5 um excess of unblended extreme-dust field dwarfs often varies and stays on the star; about half of the non-young stars with hot excess vary
abstract: Question: deep dust dimming of mature field dwarfs occurs in rare stars with extreme warm dust. Does this dust change in time, as for young extreme debris discs after giant impacts (14 of 17 vary), and is the change on the star? Method: NEOWISE 2014-2024 and AllWISE 2010 W1/W2 visit light curves of the 2,491 extreme 12 um excess candidates of a prior campaign study (213 unblended, 738 blended, 1,540 rejected), 91 known dimmers and 4,308 field-dwarf controls. A star is variable if its visit chi-square exceeds 99 percent of controls at equal W1. A new centroid test asks if the NEOWISE centroid moves with the flux, as it does when a second source in the beam varies. Results: 28 of 54 young-kinematics (52 percent) and 16 of 127 field-kinematics (13 percent) unblended stars vary, against 1.3 percent of controls and 5.6-7.0 percent of blends. For non-young unblended stars with W1-W2 excess > 0.3 mag, 12 of 26 vary against 62 of 318 blends of the same colour (p = 0.003; stratified test p = 0.015). The centroid moves in 51 of 144 variable blends but in 0 of 51 variable unblended stars (p = 1e-8), so the varying flux is on the star. With injection efficiencies, 33-65 percent of non-young hot-excess stars have excess changes of 20-50 percent rms; young stars with hot excess vary at 79 percent, like young extreme debris discs. The varying flux has W1-W2 near 0.97 mag (about 950 K). The K dwarf Gaia DR3 5628404318169472 (v_t 102 km/s) brightened by 0.3 mag at 4.6 um in 2016-2017 and faded after 2021; G4466 is recovered. Gaia DR3 1712982358083435520 (v_t 84 km/s) is a new dimmer: W1, W2 and ZTF change together and near-grey (dW2/dr 0.36). Interpretation: most genuine extreme warm dust around old field dwarfs is not a steady disc; it is made and lost within years, as after large collisions, in the same stars that dim. Limitations: blends closer than 0.1-1 arcsec pass the centroid test; 26 stars in the key group; kinematics are not ages; no spectra. citations.reason: We use its candidate list, offset classes, kinematic young weights and matched controls. The centroid test on variable flux supports its conclusion that unblended excess stars carry their own dust.
We recover the 2022 4.6 um rise of G4466 in a blind test and use its ZTF vetting flags; our population result generalises its link between dimming and variable hot dust.
We use its list of 91 main-sequence dimmers.
We compare our infrared-to-optical ratios with its in-dip NEOWISE ratios of main-sequence dippers.
